sources.title: Regional utilization survey
sources.excerpt: Across a 24-system sample, telehealth utilization remains materially above pre-2020 levels for behavioral health, medication follow-up, and chronic-care check-ins. Use is uneven in procedure-heavy specialties, but rural and mobility-limited patients continue to rely on virtual follow-up capacity.

sources.title: Earlier payer brief on reimbursement instability
sources.excerpt: An earlier payer landscape brief reported parity retrenchment across several major payer categories and warned that reimbursement for follow-up telehealth had become too unstable to justify broad service-line expansion. The brief recommended keeping behavioral-health and chronic-care telehealth growth in limited pilot mode until payment support stabilized.

sources.title: Revised payer brief on selected parity extensions
sources.excerpt: A revised payer landscape brief finds that several large commercial plans and state Medicaid programs extended payment parity for selected behavioral-health and chronic-care telehealth follow-up services through multiyear updates. For those targeted services, reimbursement support is now stable enough to justify selective expansion with payer-by-payer validation, even though parity is not universal outside the targeted lines.

sources.title: Operational compliance assessment
sources.excerpt: Multistate delivery still faces licensing, documentation, consent, and audit variability. Systems that expand telehealth successfully usually limit expansion to service lines with standardized workflows and strong compliance support.

sources.title: Access and continuity analysis
sources.excerpt: Virtual follow-up can reduce travel burden, shorten wait times, and improve continuity for behavioral-health and chronic-disease management. Patient adherence and appointment completion often improve when virtual follow-up is available.

sources.title: Cost and utilization caution memo
sources.excerpt: Utilization increases and easier access do not automatically yield system-wide savings. Some analyses find that telehealth can add demand or shift low-acuity care without offsetting downstream costs, especially when triage rules are weak.

sources.title: Clinical workflow fit note
sources.excerpt: Telehealth performs best for medication management, therapy, routine chronic-care follow-up, and monitoring. It is less appropriate for new diagnostic workups, imaging-dependent care, and complaints requiring physical examination.

sources.title: Broadband access brief
sources.excerpt: Connectivity gaps and digital literacy barriers remain concentrated in some rural and elderly populations, creating adoption limits even where demand for virtual care is strong.

sources.title: Remote patient monitoring device procurement trend
sources.excerpt: Device vendors report falling hardware costs and broader remote monitoring deployments, but the analysis focuses on capital procurement strategy rather than whether the health system should expand telehealth follow-up service lines.

sources.title: Employer benefits survey on virtual wellness perks
sources.excerpt: Employers increasingly subsidize app-based wellness services and coaching. The survey does not address clinical reimbursement, provider workflow, or the multistate health-system decision in scope.
